subject: Biology
title: How Vision Works
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: How Vision Works.

hook.text: Your eyes don't see. Your brain does. Eyes just collect light and send the data.

buildup.text: Light enters the pupil, is focused by the lens, and hits the retina at the back of the eye.

discovery.text: Rod cells detect dim light. Cone cells detect color. Together they send signals via the optic nerve.

twist.text: Your brain fills in a blind spot where the optic nerve exits the retina. You never notice the gap.

climax.text: The visual cortex assembles these signals into the seamless moving picture you experience as sight.

punchline.text: Seeing is believing—and your brain does most of it.

quiz.question: Which cells in the retina detect color?

details.summary: Vision begins when light enters the eye and stimulates photoreceptor cells in the retina. Rods detect dim light while cones detect color. The optic nerve carries signals to the visual cortex at the back of the brain, where they are assembled into conscious images.
details.whyItMatters: Vision occupies roughly 30 percent of the cortex, making it the brain's largest sensory processing system. Understanding how we see explains optical illusions, color blindness, and how visual prosthetics might restore sight.
takeaways: Rods handle dim light vision; cones handle color and detail
The visual cortex processes edges, motion, color, and depth separately
The brain constructs vision actively rather than passively recording images

faq.question: Why do optical illusions fool our eyes?
faq.answer: Illusions exploit the brain's shortcuts for interpreting visual information. The brain makes assumptions about size, depth, motion, and lighting based on experience. When these assumptions are violated, the constructed image does not match reality.

faq.question: What causes color blindness?
faq.answer: Color blindness typically results from missing or defective cone photoreceptors. Most commonly, the red or green cones malfunction due to genetic mutations on the X chromosome, which is why color blindness is far more common in males.
